findings.headline: Investment income is running £434k above budget because interest rate cuts have not materialised as expected.
findings.detail: Interest income on the council's cash balances is forecast at £1,200k against a budget of £766k. This £434k favorable variance exists only because interest rates have not fallen as anticipated when the budget was set. The council is explicitly relying on sustained high rates.
findings.matters: This income is temporary. When rates do fall—and they are expected to—this £434k will evaporate, requiring either new savings or reserve drawdown in 2027-28. It masks structural budget pressure.
findings.figures: Interest on Investments: budget £766k, forecast £1,200k, variance £434k favorable
findings.quote: Political uncertainty has delayed the reduction in forecast interest rate reductions

findings.headline: Business rates on council property have increased by £66k due to national revaluation.
findings.detail: The council's own premises business rates have been reassessed as part of the national revaluation. The increase was not reflected in the original budget, creating an unbudgeted £66k cost pressure on a £347k budget line.
findings.matters: Unforeseen property cost increases reduce financial headroom. The failure to anticipate a known national valuation process suggests gaps in budget planning.
findings.figures: Business Rates: approved budget £347k, forecast £413k, variance £66k
findings.quote: Increase in Business Rates due to National Revaluation - not reflected in Budget

findings.headline: Planning appeal costs are overrunning by £113k in the first quarter.
findings.detail: Planning Development is forecast to spend £311k against a budget of £198k. This represents a significant 57% overspend on the line, driven by planning appeal litigation costs. At this run rate, the annual overspend could reach £450k+.
findings.matters: Planning litigation costs are discretionary if development decisions are sound, or symptomatic of contested policy and weak governance if they recur. Lenders care whether cost overruns reflect operational weakness or external pressure.
findings.figures: Planning Development: approved budget £198k, forecast £311k, variance £113k
findings.quote: Planning Development expected overspend on planning appeal costs

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation programme has spent only £496k of £2.2m approved budget for 2025-28 period
findings.detail: Hart approved £1.2m for LGR costs plus a further £1m requested, totalling £2.2m across 2025-28. Actual and committed spend to date is £496k (£87k in 2025-26, £252k in 2026-27, £157k committed for 2027-28). This represents only 22% of the approved budget utilised in the first year, with £1.7m remaining to be incurred.
findings.matters: LGR is expected to deliver future efficiency savings and service changes; significant underspend relative to budget signals either delays in reorganisation delivery or better cost control, both of which affect timing of anticipated financial benefits and the council's efficiency trajectory
findings.figures: £2.2m total budget approved, £496k actual and committed spend
findings.quote: Budget Approved £1.2m with a further request for £1m in 2025/26 outturn report.

findings.paper_title: App 3 - Community Reserves – Spend Proposal for 26/27
findings.headline: Multiple projects are timed to end or transition around Local Government Reorganisation (LGR), suggesting unresolved post-LGR service continuity
findings.detail: The Locata Housing Training System is flagged as 'useful prep when LGR comes in'; the Hart's Community Garden staffing funding is being extended 'ensuring the therapeutic garden can continue into LGR'. The timing to March 2027–2028 appears deliberately aligned with LGR, but the proposals do not commit to funding beyond that point.
findings.matters: LGR represents structural uncertainty; if Hart is planning for service continuity only *into* LGR rather than beyond it, this signals either unresolved decisions about service retention post-merger or an assumption that these services will be decommissioned
findings.figures: Hart's Community Garden funding extends through March 2027 'into LGR'; Locata noted as prep for LGR; no ongoing commitments stated post-LGR
findings.quote: useful prep when LGR comes in

findings.paper_title: App 3 - Community Reserves – Spend Proposal for 26/27
findings.headline: The £700k Ukraine reserve that funds external support relies on quarterly grant payments continuing
findings.detail: The proposal to allocate £200k from the Ukraine reserve (R0043) for Ukrainian household support is conditional on grant funding that is noted as paid 'quarterly'. The reserve holds £700k currently, but its sustainability depends on external grant flows rather than council funds.
findings.matters: A major reserve (£700k) sustained by external grant funding is vulnerable to sudden cessation; if grants stop, the reserve can no longer fund the programmes it is backing, creating an unbudgeted need to find revenue or cut services
findings.figures: Ukraine reserve R0043: £700k; proposed 26/27 spend £200k (£100k to HVA, £100k to CA Hart); funded by quarterly grant payments
findings.quote: R0043 – Ukraine (£700k in this reserve and grant continues to be paid quarterly)

findings.paper_title: App 3 - Community Reserves – Spend Proposal for 26/27
findings.headline: Hart is funding recurring core staffing costs from one-off reserves across multiple years
findings.detail: Two staffing commitments from reserves extend beyond a single year: Hart's Community Garden (£40k per annum for three years) and the Here for Hart Community Grant Project Officer (£35k in both 26/27 and 27/28). Both are funded from Community Recovery and Budget Pressures reserves, not from revenue budget, creating a structural mismatch between one-off reserves and recurring salary commitments.
findings.matters: Funding permanent or multi-year posts from reserve balances is unsustainable; it suggests either hidden revenue budget pressures or unclear longer-term staffing plans, both of which create refinancing risk
findings.figures: Hart's Community Garden £40k p.a. × 3 years = £120k total; Project Officer £35k in 26/27 and £35k in 27/28
findings.quote: To support the staffing of the garden for the next 3 years; funding for staff expires March 27 £40k per annum

findings.paper_title: App 3 - Community Reserves – Spend Proposal for 26/27
findings.headline: Hart is fully depleting its £99k Community Recovery reserve on this single batch of projects
findings.detail: The proposal explicitly commits to spending all £99k of the Community Recovery reserve (R0073) across six projects: Fleet Pond wellbeing trail (£25k), Whitewater Meadow sculpture (£7k), Bramshot Farm sculpture (£17k), HVA Heroes volunteering scheme (£10k), RAF Odiham children's garden (£15k), and Hart Green Grid phase 2 (£25k). No balance is being retained.
findings.matters: Complete depletion of a reserve signals weak financial resilience; future community projects and flexibility to respond to emerging needs will depend entirely on new reserve allocation or funding
findings.figures: Community Recovery reserve R0073: £99k total; proposals total £99k (£25k+£7k+£17k+£10k+£15k+£25k)
findings.quote: The greatest demand is from the Community Recovery reserve – these proposals spend all £99k of this.

findings.headline: Planning development income surged £288k above budget from large submissions but drove service cost overruns
findings.detail: Planning development income substantially exceeded budget by £288k (actual £1.0m vs £726k budgeted), driven by large planning applications. The council's planning supplies budget also overran by £73k to handle the work, with costs including £42k planning appeal costs and £22k tree consultancy.
findings.matters: Planning fee income is volatile and driven by development activity outside the council's control. This variance masks underlying service cost volatility; future budget forecasts must stress-test this volatile income stream and the cost of responding to demand spikes.
findings.figures: £288k income over budget; £73k supplies overspend; net £215k positive variance
findings.quote: Large planning development submissions partially off-set by Agency spend.

findings.headline: Staff vacancies generated £187k savings but were partially backfilled with £77k agency cost overspend
findings.detail: The council achieved £187k in pay savings through vacancy management and staff termination payments in its £7.9m pay budget, but offset this with a £77k overspend on agency staff. This shows the council running below intended headcount and filling gaps with expensive external labour.
findings.matters: Running operations on vacancies backfilled with expensive agency staff indicates capacity constraints or recruitment difficulties. This is not sustainable—councils need matched permanent headcount to control costs and maintain service stability.
findings.figures: £187k pay savings; £77k agency overspend; agency actual £258k vs budget £181k
findings.quote: Agency costs supplement staff vacancies and support projects.

findings.headline: Waste contract overspent by £202k (6% of budget) due to new food waste collection and cost inflation
findings.detail: The waste contract exceeded budget by £202k, reaching £3.4m against a budgeted £3.2m. The overspend was driven by implementation of new food waste collection, increased National Insurance contributions, and living wage cost pressures. A £71k government grant partially offset these costs, but the underlying drivers appear structural.
findings.matters: Waste collection is a statutory, non-discretionary service under a major contract. Cost inflation here directly impacts the bottom line and foreshadows budget pressures from legislative requirements (food waste) and employment cost inflation that will likely persist.
findings.figures: £202k overspend; £3.2m budget vs £3.4m actual; £71k offsetting grant
findings.quote: Waste: increased costs due to new food waste collection + increased NI + living wage liability. There is £71k grant in income which partially off-sets increased costs.

findings.headline: Interest rate assumptions proved significantly wrong; budget assumed falling rates but rates stayed higher, benefiting outturn by £296k
findings.detail: The council's budget was set assuming interest rates would fall during 2025-26. However, "interest rates were expected to fall during 2025/26, however due to world events, interest events have remained higher than expected when setting the budget." This unexpected benefit generated £2.3m of interest income and contributed £296k to favorable outturn variance.
findings.matters: The council's budget assumptions proved unreliable. If interest rates fall to the levels originally forecast, this benefit of £296k disappears and the underlying budget position weakens, making budget forecasting reliability a concern for lenders.
findings.figures: £2.3m interest earned; £296k interest benefit in outturn variance
findings.quote: Interest rates were expected to fall during 2025/26, however due to world events, interest events have remained higher than expected when setting the budget

findings.headline: One-off £1,389k government funding adjustment from prior years significantly improved outturn but is unlikely to recur
findings.detail: Of the £1,479k improvement in outturn position compared to Q3 forecast, £1,389k came from "a one-off adjustment to core government funding from previous years." O&S Committee questioned whether "future adverse adjustments" were possible. Officers advised this relates to historic calculations and is "not expected to recur."
findings.matters: This one-off adjustment represents nearly 94% of the improved variance and will not repeat. When it falls away in future years, the underlying budget position will be weaker. The reference to possible adverse adjustments suggests the council cannot exclude further unwelcome surprises.
findings.figures: £1,389k of £1,479k improvement; approximately 94% of variance
findings.quote: Of which £1,389k has resulted from a one-off adjustment to core government funding from previous years

findings.headline: O&S Committee concerned council is drawing reserves to maintain services rather than addressing forecast budget gaps in its medium-term financial strategy
findings.detail: O&S Committee explicitly raised "concerns about drawing down reserves while the Medium-Term Financial Strategy still contained future funding pressures" and questioned "the rationale for using reserves to maintain services and fund strategic priorities rather than addressing forecast budget gaps." The council's response was that it remains "financially robust" and can "sustain current service levels until local government reorganisation in 2028," but did not address the underlying structural imbalance.
findings.matters: This suggests Hart has unresolved structural budget deficits (forecast gaps in its MTFS) which it is managing through reserve depletion rather than addressing underlying spending or income issues. This approach is temporary and unsustainable beyond 2028.
findings.figures: No specific figures; MTFS is described as containing "future funding pressures" and "forecast budget gaps"
findings.quote: Concerns about drawing down reserves while the Medium-Term Financial Strategy still contained future funding pressures

findings.headline: Prudent minimum working balance reduced from £6m to £5m to fund LGR costs during a period of budget uncertainty
findings.detail: The council's prudent minimum working balance was set at £6m in 2023. To fund the additional LGR allocation, this minimum is being reduced to £5m. The council explicitly notes this figure "may need to be lowered if major budget pressures arise."
findings.matters: The council is reducing its financial buffer at a time when structural budget pressures exist (O&S Committee identified MTFS gaps) and major reorganisation costs are uncertain and likely to increase further.
findings.figures: Prudent minimum being lowered from £6m to £5m; revised balance after transfers will be approximately £5m
findings.quote: This would require the lowering of the prudent minimum working balance to £5m. Council noted that this figure may need to be lowered if major budget pressures arise.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs are likely to significantly exceed the initial £1m reserve allocation
findings.detail: Hart is being absorbed into a new unitary authority on 31 March 2028. The council initially set aside £1m for LGR transition costs, but this paper states costs are "likely to be significantly more than this" based on mobilisation meetings. An additional £1m transfer to the LGR reserve is now proposed, with the council acknowledging that "as LGR develops, the costs will become clearer and this position can be adjusted if necessary," implying further increases are likely.
findings.matters: This represents substantial uncertain costs being funded from reserves at a time when the council faces structural budget gaps (per O&S Committee). Lenders may be concerned about the council's ability to absorb escalating reorganisation costs.
findings.figures: Initial £1m allocation; additional £1m now proposed; total LGR reserve rising to £2m; actual costs described as "likely to be significantly more"
findings.quote: Hart's LGR pre-vesting day costs are likely to be significantly more than this

findings.headline: Unbudgeted £77k Ground Maintenance Embedded Lease incurred
findings.detail: Ground Maintenance Embedded Lease (project 1613) had zero initial budget but resulted in £77k actual expenditure, marked Complete. This represents capital-type spending approved outside the formal budget cycle.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted capital commitments indicate incomplete forecasting or emergency decisions, either of which affects lenders' confidence in financial planning and control.
findings.figures: £0 budgeted, £77k spent
findings.quote: 1613 Ground Maintenance Embedded Lease 0 0 0 0 77 77 Complete

findings.headline: £725k temporary accommodation housing project entirely deferred to 2026-27
findings.detail: The Temporary Accommodation 3x2 bed houses project was deferred in full to the following year, with Cabinet agreement in March 2026. Zero was spent in 2025-26 against an approved budget of £725k.
findings.matters: Housing supply is a council priority and lenders assess housing delivery as indicator of execution capacity and financial health; significant deferrals suggest delivery constraints.
findings.figures: £725k approved budget, £0 outturn, £725k carried forward
findings.quote: 1617 Temporary Accommodation 3x2bed houses 1 725 0 (725) 0 0 0 C/F- agreed

findings.headline: Kingsway Flood Alleviation Scheme cancelled with £138k unspent
findings.detail: A flood management capital project budgeted at £138k from carry-forwards was cancelled in 2025-26 with no explanation in the document. It is the only scheme explicitly marked Cancelled in the capital schedule.
findings.matters: Flood alleviation schemes are typically regulatory-driven environmental infrastructure; unexplained cancellation suggests changed risk appetite or constrained resources affecting council strategy.
findings.figures: £138k budgeted, £0 outturn, £138k variance
findings.quote: 1614 Kingsway Flood Alleviation Sch 0 138 0 138 0 (138) Cancelled

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 25-26 May publication draft
findings.headline: Whistleblowing case identified areas requiring governance improvement
findings.detail: One whistleblowing case was reported during 2025/26. When considered by the Audit Committee in March 2026, 'an action plan approved to address areas where improvement is needed'. This suggests the whistleblowing governance process or investigation had gaps requiring remediation.
findings.matters: Whistleblowing governance weaknesses suggest potential issues with how misconduct and fraud concerns are being surfaced and handled; this affects fraud risk management.
findings.figures: One whistleblowing case reported in 2025/26
findings.quote: the outcome of the only case reported under the policy in the financial year was considered by the Committee in March 2026, with an action plan approved to address areas where improvement is needed.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 25-26 May publication draft
findings.headline: Senior Leadership Team restructured July 2025 with formal governance action to ensure capacity during Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: Hart restructured its Senior Leadership Team in July 2025 with 'residual capacity assessed and deputy arrangements put in place'. A governance improvement action has been added specifically 'in light of LGR and the SLT restructure in July 2025, ensure effective leadership and management capacity across the council's services' due throughout 2026/27.
findings.matters: Leadership capacity and continuity directly affect decision-making quality and service delivery; LGR creates additional organizational demands during a leadership transition, and capacity constraints could affect council stability.
findings.figures: SLT restructured July 2025; improvement action due throughout 2026/27
findings.quote: The Senior Leadership Team was restructured in July 2025 with residual capacity assessed and deputy arrangements put in place.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 25-26 May publication draft
findings.headline: Internal Audit management action recommendations not being implemented within agreed timescales
findings.detail: The Audit Committee noted in March 2026 that management is not consistently implementing internal audit recommendations by the timescales they have agreed to. This has been identified as a governance improvement issue requiring managers to 'better assess realistic deadlines when they agree and sign off the management actions in IA reports'.
findings.matters: Failure to implement audit recommendations on time indicates weak management discipline and suggests identified control weaknesses are not being fixed, which increases underlying control risk.
findings.figures: Issue noted Audit Committee March 2026; improvement actions due throughout 2026/27
findings.quote: Internal audits management actions are not all being implemented within agreed timescales, as noted by Audit Committee in March 2026

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 25-26 May publication draft
findings.headline: Finance system implementation ongoing with final phases and AI module due December 2026
findings.detail: Hart implemented a new financial system during 2025/26. Internal Audit has reviewed key aspects with positive outcomes reported. However, governance improvement action plan identifies that 'final phases, including AI module, are completed on time and on budget with robust controls across all modules' as a priority with December 2026 completion target, indicating implementation is not yet complete.
findings.matters: Incomplete finance system implementation with major modules still pending creates risk to financial reporting accuracy and timeliness; major modules like an AI component add complexity to controls.
findings.figures: New system implemented 2025/26; final phases and AI module due Dec 2026
findings.quote: A new financial system was implemented during 2025/26, key aspects of which have been subject to assurance reviews by Internal Audit, with positive outcomes reported.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 25-26 May publication draft
findings.headline: External auditors gave a qualified audit opinion on 2024/25 accounts
findings.detail: EY completed Hart's 2024/25 accounts audit on a 'qualified' basis due to the government's reset approach to clear backlogs. Despite the qualified opinion, EY's Value for Money conclusion was positive, finding the Council has proper arrangements to plan and manage resources, make informed decisions, and manage risks.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion is a material concern for lenders and indicates auditor reservations about the accounts or control environment; understanding the nature of the qualification is essential for credit decisions.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit completed on qualified basis; EY Value for Money conclusion positive
findings.quote: The external Auditors, EY, have now concluded their 2024/25 accounts audit, although it was completed on a 'qualified' audit basis due to the ongoing impact of the government's 'reset' approach to clear backlogs.

findings.headline: No value-for-money significant weaknesses identified, but auditor notes ongoing need for governance improvements on cyber security and risk register timeliness
findings.detail: The auditor confirmed no significant weaknesses in arrangements for financial sustainability, governance, or improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. However, the Annual Governance Statement discloses ongoing improvements needed: 'timely completion of audits due to sector-wide resource constraints, enhancement of risk registers to reflect emerging financial and operational risks and strengthening cyber security controls in line with national guidance.'
findings.matters: While the clean VFM conclusion is positive, the disclosed gaps in cyber security and risk register timeliness are emerging governance risks. Cyber incidents or unidentified financial risks could crystallise quickly.
findings.figures: Four Audit Committee meetings held in 2024/25; no outstanding VFM recommendations from prior years
findings.quote: However, areas for improvement disclosed in the AGS include timely completion of audits due to sector-wide resource constraints, enhancement of risk registers to reflect emerging financial and operational risks and strengthening cyber security controls in line with national guidance.

findings.headline: Pension liability disclosure error of £764k in fair value of pension assets, though no impact on reported liability
findings.detail: The auditor identified a £764k misstatement in disclosures relating to the closing fair value of pension assets and asset ceiling effect. Although this had no impact on the reported pension liability in the accounts, it suggests a gap in the quality of pension accounting data preparation.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are often a council's largest off-balance-sheet exposure. Disclosure errors signal weak internal controls over actuarial data reconciliation, which could mask larger errors in the liability valuation itself.
findings.figures: £764k misstatement in pension asset fair value disclosure
findings.quote: As part of our testing, we identified one misstatement in the disclosures relating to the closing fair value of pension assets and asset ceiling effect, amounting to £764k but this has no impact on the reported pension liability in the accounts.

findings.headline: Serco waste contract extended for 8 years from October 2025, but new government waste legislation creates contract performance uncertainty
findings.detail: The council and partner Basingstoke & Deane Borough Council have agreed an 8-year extension with Serco from 1 October 2025. The original main contract was due to end mid-2026. However, the auditor notes: 'due to new government legislation, there is uncertainty on waste services moving forward' and this has been flagged in the council's risk register. The extended contract represents a major fixed cost commitment in an environment of legislative flux.
findings.matters: Waste services are a material council cost. An 8-year commitment to Serco locks the council into a single provider and cost structure during a period when central government is reshaping waste policy (e.g., Extended Producer Responsibility). Changes to waste legislation could create unfunded burdens or stranded contract costs.
findings.figures: 8-year contract extension from 1 October 2025; original contract end date was mid-2026
findings.quote: The main contract with Serco is due to end midway through 2026, and due to new government legislation, there is uncertainty on waste services moving forward. This has been identified in their Risk Register as discussed earlier in this document, with The Council, in partnership with Basingstoke and Deane Borough Council, has agreed an 8-year extension with Serco from 1 Oct 2025.

findings.headline: Reliance on sustained savings delivery to balance budget: £2.1m in 2024/25, £1.2m planned for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council balanced its 2025/26 budget through application of £6.5m of savings and mitigations without drawing unallocated reserves. This follows delivery of £2.1m savings in 2024/25. The 2025/26 savings target of £1.274m is dependent on identified measures: food waste funding (£0.8m), 2.99% council tax (£0.3m), and senior leadership vacancy management (£0.15m), with a gap of £1.2m still to be identified.
findings.matters: Councils that rely on continuous savings programmes risk service quality degradation and stumbling if headcount reductions or income measures hit implementation obstacles. Hart's track record of delivery is solid, but the forward gap of £1.2m in 2025/26 is not yet closed.
findings.figures: £2.1m savings delivered 2024/25; £1.274m target for 2025/26; £1.2m of 2025/26 target still to be identified
findings.quote: The 2025/26 Budget has been balanced through the application of £6.5 million of savings and mitigations, without the need to drawdown from unallocated reserves.

findings.headline: Treasury income pressure of up to £150k annually from expected interest rate changes
findings.detail: The council's MTFS identifies a forecast reduction in treasury investment returns due to expected interest rate changes, with budgeted pressure of £150k in 2026/27 and £100k in 2028/29. This reflects the impact of holding £42.1m in investments at lower yields as rates fall, creating a structural income headwind.
findings.matters: Treasury income has been a material positive contributor to the council's financial position (£715k gain in 2024/25). Future reliance on investment returns is now at risk, removing a buffer that has helped absorb other pressures.
findings.figures: £42.1m total investments held; treasury income pressure of £150k (2026/27) and £100k (2028/29) forecast
findings.quote: Key challenges for 2025/26 include inflationary impacts on service costs, increased employer National Insurance contributions of approximately £300k, and new obligations such as the rollout of food waste collection and preparation for potential local government reorganisation, forecast reduction in treasury investment returns due to expected interest rate changes, adding £150k pressure in 2026/27 and £100k in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Investment property valuation overstatement of £1.244m identified and corrected in audit
findings.detail: During audit testing of a sample of investment properties, the auditor identified one property with an overstatement in valuation requiring a £1.244m correction, which management agreed. While the auditor concluded this does not indicate a material weakness in controls, it demonstrates a valuation quality control gap on a significant asset class.
findings.matters: Investment properties are material to balance sheet presentation and fund availability. A £1.2m error that survived internal review before audit suggests control gaps in asset valuation governance.
findings.figures: £1.244m overstatement correction on investment property
findings.quote: As part of our testing, we identified one audit difference within the sample of properties reviewed. The audit difference related to an overstatement in valuation and required a correction of £1,244k which has been agreed by the management.

findings.headline: Structural funding gap of £2.4m forecast for 2026/27–2028/29 despite delivering savings
findings.detail: The council's Medium-Term Financial Strategy projects a structural funding gap even after applying annual council tax increases at 2.99% and implementing savings. The gaps are £1.4m (2026/27), £0.6m (2027/28), and £0.4m (2028/29), totalling £2.4m. Drivers include inflationary cost pressures, increased employer National Insurance contributions (~£300k), treasury investment return reductions (£150k in 2026/27, £100k in 2028/29), and new statutory burdens such as food waste collection and local government reorganisation preparation.
findings.matters: A structural gap of this size, persisting across the medium term, signals that the council cannot rely on one-off savings or reserves to balance its budget sustainably. This requires meaningful service change or further income generation.
findings.figures: Cumulative shortfall of £2.4m over 2026/27–2028/29; 2.99% council tax rise generates additional £254k in 2025/26, rising to £280k by 2028/29
findings.quote: The MTFS projects a structural funding gap from 2026/27 onwards, even after applying annual council tax increases of 2.99%. The residual gaps are £1.4m in 2026/27, £0.6m in 2027/28, and £0.4m in 2028/29. This results in a cumulative shortfall of £2.4m over the period.

findings.headline: Qualified opinion on financial statements with multi-year assurance gaps on historical property valuations
findings.detail: The auditor issued a qualified opinion on 2024/25 accounts (progress from prior-year disclaimers on 2023/24 and 2022/23). However, due to gaps in assurance over Property, Plant and Equipment valued in 2022/23, the auditor cannot verify all opening balances, in-year movements, and 2024/25 comparative balances. The auditor states: 'we do not have assurance over some brought forward balances from 2023/24 where we did not gain assurance (the opening balances). This means we do not have assurance over all 2024/25 in-year movements and the comparative prior year movements.'
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in the reliability of financial statements. Unresolved audit gaps on asset valuations and opening balances limit confidence in reported position and comparability across years.
findings.figures: PPE valuation issues from 2022/23 remain unresolved; forecast to move to unqualified opinion by 2026/27 per LARRIG01 recovery plan
findings.quote: Although the level of assurance gained has increased, we have not yet obtained sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances.

findings.headline: Capital spending £3.5m under budget (42% underspend), driven by supplier resource issues and project approval delays
findings.detail: Capital forecast £4.9m against £8.4m budget. Delays include Edenbrook car park (supplier resourcing problems), Frogmore heat pump (Cabinet approval delayed to January 2026), and cascade delays on solar and insulation schemes. The scale of underspend suggests execution challenges.
findings.matters: Large capital underspends and delays indicate delivery risk and reduce planned service improvements or efficiency gains; concentrated carry-forwards into 26/27 increase next year's execution pressure
findings.figures: £3.5m underspend on £8.4m budget; Edenbrook £144k carry forward; Frogmore heat pump £1,159k carry forward
findings.quote: Capital projects are forecast to be £3.5m less than budget, mainly due to rescheduling into 26/27. The external supplier selected to deliver this project has experienced resourcing problems.

findings.headline: Income forecast revised down £202k from Q2, with planning development, building control, and grants all underperforming
findings.detail: Three income streams were revised downward from Q2: planning development -£80k, building control -£40k, grants -£78k. While the Q3 outturn remains positive overall, these downward revisions indicate income is not tracking expectations and future income reliability is uncertain.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on stable, predictable income to support debt servicing; repeated downward forecast revisions create uncertainty for future cash flow
findings.figures: Planning development -£80k, building control -£40k, grants -£78k; total -£202k
findings.quote: Income: -£202k : Planning development -£80k, building control -£40k, grants -£78k

findings.headline: Council deliberately depleting reserves to maintain £25.9m under-borrowed position, betting on interest rates to fall by mid-2027.
findings.detail: Hart is not undertaking new borrowing despite a capital financing requirement of £39.9m (2024/25), instead funding capital expenditure from capital receipts, grants, and reserves. The paper explicitly describes this as deliberate: reserves are being used 'as a temporary measure' while awaiting interest rate falls. Treasury advisors (MUFG) forecast Bank Rate to fall to 3.25% by Q3 2027 and PWLB 5-year certainty rates to fall from current 4.78% to 4.20% by Q2 2027. As a result, fund balances are declining from £53.2m (2024/25) to £38.1m (2028/29) — a £15.1m reduction over four years. Zero borrowing is planned for any year through 2028/29.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand refinancing risk. The strategy depends entirely on specific interest rate forecasts. If rates don't fall as expected, the council will face higher borrowing costs when it eventually refinances, and reserve depletion limits flexibility for unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing £25,885k (2024/25); fund balances declining £53,166k to £38,097k; external debt £14,079k (31/03/2025) declining to £13,624k (30/11/2025); borrowing requirement £0 for 2026/27–2028/29; PWLB 5-year currently 4.78%, forecast 4.20%; Bank Rate currently 4%, forecast 3.25%.
findings.quote: The council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.headline: £1m from unallocated general fund reserves earmarked for local government reorganisation transition costs
findings.detail: Hart is drawing £1m from its unallocated working balance to fund LGR transition costs: redundancies, TUPE transfers, IT system integration, asset rationalization, and backfilling of seconded staff. This is happening while the council faces a forecast budget deficit ahead, consuming reserves at a time of structural pressure.
findings.matters: Large one-time cost from already-constrained reserves at a moment of financial vulnerability, reducing the council's flexibility to respond to the forecast deficit
findings.figures: £1m from unallocated general fund balance; LGR costs described as 'significant'
findings.quote: It is now essential in setting the budget and MTFS to earmark £1m from the unallocated general fund balance for this purpose.

findings.headline: Core government grant funding declining by £1.2m over the MTFS period
findings.detail: Hart's core government grant is falling from £4,656k (2024/25) to £3,455k (2028/29)—a structural reduction of £1.2m. The council receives transitional funding protection for three years (ending 2028/29), but the new Fair Funding formula delivers substantially lower baseline funding thereafter.
findings.matters: Structural decline in core government funding means the council faces permanent loss of revenue with limited flexibility to recover it
findings.quote: The Government has provided a three-year funding settlement... Transitional funding is provided for 3 years with the 2028/29 fair funding amount being the new funding level

findings.headline: Commercial property income increasingly critical to budget but exposed to void risk
findings.detail: Hart's budget includes £1.17m in investment property rental income. The council acknowledges property is 'an increasingly important revenue stream' but faces risk of rent loss from void periods. CIPFA's Financial Resilience Index identifies Hart as having 'relatively low ratio of income from fees and charges to total service expenditure'—the only higher-risk area identified for the council.
findings.matters: Uncertain, volatile income stream is critical to budget balance; void periods or tenant loss could worsen the forecast deficit
findings.figures: £1.17m investment property rental income; void risk identified as key MTFS risk
findings.quote: Property – this is an increasingly important revenue stream in the Council's budget, so the risk of rent loss due to void periods must be evaluated.

findings.headline: Waste contract cost increased by £1.3m due to statutory weekly food waste requirement, with uncertain government compensation
findings.detail: The Environment Act requires weekly food waste collection. Hart's waste contract cost has increased by £1.3m to implement this mandate. Government promised new burdens funding to cover costs but is not delivering it. The council is using Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) funding—a business tax on waste packaging—to partly cover the cost, but EPR is uncertain and subject to future changes.
findings.matters: A large, non-discretionary cost increase driven by statute has no guaranteed funding, creating operational and financial risk
findings.figures: £1.3m annual waste cost increase; using up to £1m EPR in 2026/27 (uncertain), with £0.5m in revenue budget and balance transferred to contingency reserve
findings.quote: The annual cost of the waste/recycling contract has increased by £1.3m, primarily due to the statutory requirement to implement weekly food waste collections.

findings.headline: £1.5m of promised government funding for new burdens and National Insurance now not delivered
findings.detail: The Council anticipated £1m in new burdens funding for weekly food waste collections and £70k in ongoing National Insurance compensation. These have now been 'theoretically rolled into the overall funding settlement', meaning councils won't receive the promised funding. This creates a recurring structural shortfall.
findings.matters: A £1.5m recurring revenue gap that was promised but not delivered represents a material and permanent loss of income
findings.figures: £1.5m pa compared to 2024/25 budget; £85k net reduction in core grant 2025/26 to 2026/27
findings.quote: Compared to the 2024/25 budget, these two factors alone have increased the Council's costs by £1.5m pa with no specific funding being received as promised.

findings.headline: MTFS forecasts a significant budget shortfall from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: While the 2026/27 budget balances, Hart's Medium-Term Financial Strategy shows a 'significant budget shortfall' from 2027/28. This unsustainability is evident in the council already freezing fees (green waste, car parking) and withdrawing reserves for one-off costs, signalling the current position cannot hold.
findings.matters: A forecast deficit makes a council unsellable to lenders and signals imminent need for service reductions or reserves depletion
findings.figures: Core Spending Power declining from £13,775k (2026/27) to £13,687k (2027/28) and £13,581k (2028/29); grant funding drops £388k in 2027/28 and £404k in 2028/29
findings.quote: the MTFS is currently showing a significant budget shortfall in 2027/28 and beyond so reserves will need to be reviewed alongside the budget setting process.

findings.headline: The council is prohibited from borrowing to invest in land or buildings for yield, with PWLB repayment and access penalties for non-compliance.
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states that restrictions on council borrowing prohibit investments in land or buildings for yield. No yield-based investments are allowed in Hart's capital programme for three years, with no alternative financing options. The council understands that non-compliance will result in repayment of PWLB borrowing and may prevent future access to PWLB.
findings.matters: Lenders to local government need to understand what borrowing options are available to a council and what constraints apply. These PWLB restrictions directly limit Hart's ability to pursue commercial income strategies through capital investments, which affects the council's financial flexibility and revenue options.
findings.figures: three years
findings.quote: Restrictions on council borrowing prohibit investments in land or buildings for yield. No yield-based investments are allowed in the Capital Programme for three years, and no alternative financing options. Non-compliance will result in repayment of PWLB borrowing and may prevent future access to PWLB.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: External debt declining steadily with substantial spare borrowing capacity, indicating strong de-leveraging and balance sheet health.
findings.detail: The council's external debt is forecast to decline from £14,079k (2024/25 actual) through £13,711k (2025/26) to £12,951k by 2027/28. Debt reduction is steady at £361k–£384k annually, while the council maintains £25,557k of under-borrowing.
findings.matters: Steady debt reduction and substantial spare capacity demonstrate manageable debt service and low refinancing risk, supporting credit quality for lenders.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Entire capital programme financed from earmarked reserves and grants, with zero borrowing requirement despite £25.6m of spare capacity.
findings.detail: Capital financing of £6,818k comes entirely from earmarked reserves (£3,969k) and capital grants (£2,845k), with no borrowing drawn. The council has £25,557k of under-borrowing against its £46m operational boundary, but is choosing not to use it for capital investment.
findings.matters: Reliance on earmarked reserves erodes the council's financial buffers and flexibility, while the absence of capital borrowing despite available capacity suggests either constrained investment appetite or precautionary financial positioning.
findings.figures: Earmarked Reserves £3,969k, Capital grants £2,845k, Borrowing requirement £0, Available spare capacity £25,557k
findings.quote: Earmarked Reserves 5,160  544  3,969; Borrowing requirement 0  0  0

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Capital expenditure budget revised down by £793k in-year, with actual spend at only 22% of original estimate by end of Q2.
findings.detail: The capital programme was revised from originally planned £7,611k down to £6,818k. As of 30 September 2025, only £1,485k has been spent. With six months of the financial year passed, actual spend against the original budget is tracking significantly below proportionate progress, signalling either project delays or reduced scope.
findings.matters: Substantial under-spending at mid-year indicates either delivery risk or a tighter capital investment discipline; either way, it signals potential pressure on the council's strategic capital plans.
findings.figures: Original estimate £7,611k, revised estimate £6,818k, actual spend £1,485k as of 30/09/2025
findings.quote: Total capital expenditure       7,611 1,485  6,818

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Frogmore LC Heat Pumps (PSDS-funded decarbonisation scheme) forecast at 23% of budget, concentrating 81% of total capital variance
findings.detail: The Frogmore LC - Heat Pumps project has a revised budget of £1,300k but is forecast to spend only £302k in 2025/26, with £998k deferred to 2026/27. This single scheme accounts for £998k of the £1,225k capital programme underspend.
findings.matters: Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme funding carries strict compliance and spend-timing requirements; material year-on-year slippage poses risk of grant clawback and signals project delivery concerns
findings.figures: Budget £1,300k; 25/26 forecast £302k (23%); 26/27 budget £998k; variance £998k
findings.quote: Frogmore LC  - Heat Pumps (PSDS) 1 0 1,300 0 1,300 302 (998)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Capital programme forecast to underspend by £1.2m, a 13.8% variance against £8.8m revised budget
findings.detail: The capital projects budget of £8,842k is forecast to deliver only £7,617k of spend, a variance of (£1,225k). This represents material shortfall across 28 community and corporate capital projects.
findings.matters: Significant capital programme underspend indicates either forecast unreliability or project delivery challenges; lenders assess whether councils can reliably execute capital investment plans
findings.figures: £8,842k revised budget vs £7,617k forecast = £1,225k variance (13.8%)

findings.paper_title: Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Capital projects are delayed, with £1.2m of planned spending pushed into 2026/27
findings.detail: Capital expenditure forecast at £6.8m against budget of £8.0m. The paper attributes this to 'delays into 26/27' but provides no detail on which projects, why they are delayed, or whether delivery risk exists.
findings.matters: Persistent capital delivery delays can indicate capacity constraints or project management weakness, and may affect the council's ability to deliver planned infrastructure improvements.
findings.figures: £1.2m underspend (15% of capital budget)
findings.quote: Capital projects are forecast to be £1.2m less than budget, mainly due to delays into 26/27.

findings.paper_title: Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Employee costs are £378k higher than budgeted with no explanation offered
findings.detail: The forecast identifies employee costs as a £378k variance against budget. This is a material cost pressure (2.7% of total net service costs) but the paper does not explain whether this is one-off or structural, or what has driven it. The paper also notes waste contract costs up £110k.
findings.matters: Unexplained structural payroll increases of this scale suggest either unbudgeted staffing changes, pay inflation, or service pressures that could persist and affect the council's financial sustainability and borrowing requirement.
findings.figures: Employee costs £378k; total net cost of service underspend only £611k despite this increase
findings.quote: Employee costs £378k

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Leadership restructuring is dependent on employee vacancies materialising to fund reorganisation costs.
findings.detail: The council notes that the new leadership team restructuring will incur "further costs yet to be incurred but will be met by vacancy savings". The council is currently showing a £378k underspend in employee costs, partly due to £355k in pay cost vacancies. The restructuring is being funded by the assumption these vacancies continue.
findings.matters: If employee vacancies do not materialise or the restructuring costs exceed expectations, there is no budget buffer to absorb the overspend, creating a risk to the council's outturn.
findings.figures: £378k pay cost underspend; £355k vacancies; Leadership team £45k underspend
findings.quote: Reflecting new leadership team. Further costs yet to be incurred but will be met by vacancy savings.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Planning appeal costs of £112k suggest significant number of contested planning decisions.
findings.detail: Planning development shows £112k in planning appeal costs, with an additional £70k for tree consultancy. The council has reallocated consultancy budget from the central pot to cover these costs. The overall planning budget remains under control, but the volume and cost of appeals is material.
findings.matters: High planning appeal costs indicate the council's planning decisions are being contested in significant numbers; this can signal either policy disputes with developers or pressure from intensive development activity in the area.
findings.figures: £112k planning appeal costs; £70k tree consultancy reallocation
findings.quote: Planning appeal costs £112k - consultancy budget moved from central pot. £70k for tree consultancy which is off-set by vacancy savings.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand is rising, with costs forecast to exceed budget by £55k and budget reallocated from housing need grants.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation is forecast to cost £320k against a revised budget of £265k (£55k overspend). The council has reallocated budget from housing need grants to meet these costs and explicitly describes the service as "demand led" and "subject to fluctuations". This signals growing homelessness pressure in the area and an unpredictable cost stream.
findings.matters: Demand-led homelessness costs often reflect wider economic stress in the community and are notoriously difficult to forecast; growing temporary accommodation is a leading indicator of financial hardship among residents.
findings.figures: £320k forecast vs £265k revised budget (£55k overspend); budget moved from housing need grant
findings.quote: This is partially off-set by temporary accomodation costs. Demand led service - subject to fluctuations.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Q2 Forecast 2025/26 Revenue, Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: New waste contract is delivering cost overruns from national insurance and living wage inflation.
findings.detail: The waste contract shows a £91k overspend (£3,292k forecast vs £3,201k budget). The council explicitly notes this is driven by "increased NI + living wage costs associated with 6 months of the new waste contract". Since this represents only the first six months, the full-year impact will be significantly larger, indicating a structural cost pressure that will persist for the contract duration.
findings.matters: Waste is a major operational cost with limited control; the council has locked into a contract that is already delivering inflation-driven cost overruns, creating a structural budget pressure for future years.
findings.figures: £91k overspend; 6 months of contract already showing inflation impact
findings.quote: Waste: these costs reflect increased NI + living wage costs associated with 6 months of the new waste contract.

news_drafts.headline: Investment income is running £434k above budget because interest rate cuts have not materialised as expected.
news_drafts.lead: This income is temporary. When rates do fall—and they are expected to—this £434k will evaporate, requiring either new savings or reserve drawdown in 2027-28. It masks structural budget pressure.

news_drafts.headline: Business rates on council property have increased by £66k due to national revaluation.
news_drafts.lead: Unforeseen property cost increases reduce financial headroom. The failure to anticipate a known national valuation process suggests gaps in budget planning.

news_drafts.headline: Planning appeal costs are overrunning by £113k in the first quarter.
news_drafts.lead: Planning litigation costs are discretionary if development decisions are sound, or symptomatic of contested policy and weak governance if they recur. Lenders care whether cost overruns reflect operational weakness or external pressure.
